951	\section{Proposition Proofs}
952	\label{app:proofs}
953	
954	\textbf{Proof of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}} (Routing Information Loss Under RevIN, revised form).
955	
956	\begin{proof}
957	Throughout, $X$ denotes a raw window, $(M,\Sigma)$ its per-window mean/scale, $S = (X-M)/\Sigma$ its RevIN-normalized shape, and $E$ a deterministic (possibly randomized) router assignment. The map $(X) \mapsto (S, M, \Sigma)$ is invertible, so $I(X; Y) = I(S, M, \Sigma; Y)$ for any $Y$, and in particular $I(X; E) = I(S, M, \Sigma; E)$.
958	
959	\emph{Part (i): Exact decomposition.} By the chain rule of mutual information applied to $(S, M, \Sigma; E)$,
960	\begin{align*}
961	I(X; E) \;=\; I(S, M, \Sigma;\, E) \;=\; I(S;\, E) + I(M, \Sigma;\, E \mid S).
962	\end{align*}
963	Rearranging, $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma;\, E \mid S) \geq 0$. This identity holds \emph{without any independence assumption} between $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$.
964	
965	\emph{Part (ii): Unconditional quantitative bound.} We bound the conditional mutual information $I(M,\Sigma; E \mid S)$ from below in terms of the \emph{unconditional} quantities $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ and $I(M,\Sigma; S)$. Applying the chain rule two different ways to $I(M,\Sigma; E, S)$,
966	\begin{align*}
967	I(M,\Sigma;\, E, S) &= I(M,\Sigma;\, S) + I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \qquad\text{(expand $S$ first)} \\
968	                    &= I(M,\Sigma;\, E) + I(M,\Sigma;\, S \mid E) \qquad\text{(expand $E$ first).}
969	\end{align*}
970	Equating and solving for $I(M,\Sigma; E \mid S)$,
971	\[
972	I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \;=\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S) \;+\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S \mid E).
973	\]
974	Since $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E) \geq 0$ (mutual information is non-negative), we obtain
975	\[
976	I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;=\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \;\geq\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S),
977	\]
978	where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M,\Sigma; S) \geq 0$ is the \emph{leakage} of location-scale statistics into the shape. Equality (tightness) holds iff $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E) = 0$, i.e.\ iff $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$ are conditionally independent given $E$. In particular, unconditional independence $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ implies $\varepsilon = 0$ and recovers the classical $I(X;E) - I(S;E) \geq I(M,\Sigma; E)$ bound as a corollary.
979	
980	\emph{Part (iii): Full-information corner.} Suppose the router depends entirely on the stripped statistics: $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M, \Sigma)$, which means $p(E \mid S, M, \Sigma) = p(E \mid M, \Sigma)$. Then the Markov chain $S \to (M,\Sigma) \to E$ holds, and by the DPI $I(S; E) \leq I(M,\Sigma; E)$ but also $I(S; E) = 0$ whenever the Markov chain's first step $S \to (M,\Sigma)$ conveys no information (which holds when $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$). In the full-information corner case $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ and $E$ determined by $(M,\Sigma)$, we have $I(S;E) = 0$ and $I(X;E) = I(M,\Sigma;E) = H(E) - H(E \mid M,\Sigma) = H(E)$. Hence $I(X;E) - I(S;E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution.
981	
982	\emph{Part (iv): Empirical leakage and signal ratio.} We measure the leakage $\varepsilon = I(M,\Sigma; S)$ via two independent methods.
983	
984	\emph{Gaussian reference.} Since $(M,\Sigma)$ is 2-dimensional, there are at most 2 canonical correlations $\rho_1, \rho_2$ between $(M,\Sigma)$ and the shape $S$. For jointly Gaussian variables, $I(M,\Sigma; S) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^2 \log(1 - \rho_i^2)$. This yields $\varepsilon_\text{Gauss}$ ranging from $0.09$ nats (Weather, $\rho_\text{max}{=}0.35$) to $1.26$ nats (Exchange, $\rho_\text{max}{=}0.89$). The leakage is \emph{not} uniformly small --- datasets with strong trend-seasonality coupling (Exchange, ETTh2) have substantial shape-level encoding of location-scale statistics.
985	
986	\emph{Distribution-free cross-check.} Because canonical correlations capture only linear dependence, we cross-validate with the KSG $k$-nearest-neighbor MI estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}, which requires no distributional assumptions. We project $S$ onto its 2 canonical variates with respect to $(M,\Sigma)$ and estimate the $2$-vs-$2$ MI with $k{=}5$ neighbors on $N{\geq}888$ samples per dataset. The KSG estimates agree with the Gaussian reference within $\pm 0.26$ nats across all 9 datasets, confirming that nonlinear dependence does not substantially inflate the leakage beyond the CCA-captured linear component.
987	
988	\emph{Tightness condition.} The bound~(ii) is informative when $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$. Since $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ increases with the location-scale variance, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ is a monotone proxy for the tightness of the bound. This explains the $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ correlation: high-$R$ datasets (Exchange, $R{=}2.17$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$, producing large gains ($-68.5\%$); low-$R$ datasets (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \approx \varepsilon$, producing no gain ($+2.9\%$).
989	\end{proof}
990	
991	\textbf{Remark on the classical form.} The earlier version assumed $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ outright. The revised form~(ii) keeps $\varepsilon$ explicit and Part~(iv) measures it via both parametric (CCA) and non-parametric (KSG) methods, eliminating the independence assumption. Part~(v) bypasses the bound entirely by directly measuring $H(E \mid S)$, confirming the gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats (Table~\ref{tab:mi_tightness}). The agreement between Gaussian reference and distribution-free KSG estimates ($\pm 0.26$ nats) confirms the CCA-based values are reliable despite non-Gaussianity.
992	
993	\subsection{Theoretical Depth of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}}
994	\label{app:prop2_depth}
995	
996	While the MI decomposition in Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} is algebraically a chain-rule identity, it has deeper information-theoretic content when connected to rate-distortion theory and phase transitions.
997	
998	\textbf{Rate-distortion interpretation of $R(\mathcal{D})$.}
999	Instance normalization is a \emph{deterministic lossy compression}: it maps $X \mapsto S$, discarding $(M, \Sigma)$. In rate-distortion theory~\citep{cover2006elements}, this compression has rate $R_\text{strip} = I(X; M, \Sigma \mid S)$ and distortion (for routing) $D_\text{route} = H(E \mid S) - H(E \mid X) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S)$, which is exactly Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i). Under Gaussianity, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ is proportional to the rate-distortion slope at the normalization operating point: it measures how much routing capacity is consumed by the statistics that normalization strips. Specifically, if the joint $(M, \Sigma, S)$ is multivariate Gaussian, then $I(M, \Sigma; E) \propto \log(1 + R(\mathcal{D}))$ (by the Gaussian mutual information formula), making $R(\mathcal{D})$ a \emph{monotone surrogate for the bits lost to normalization}. The validated $\rho = -0.88$ correlation (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}) is thus not a statistical coincidence but a consequence of this rate-distortion structure.
1000	
1001	\begin{proposition}[Phase Transition in Routing Quality]
1002	\label{prop:phase_transition}
1003	Consider a softmax router on the interpolated input $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{raw} + \alpha\,\mathrm{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{raw})$. Under the Gaussian model with approximately orthogonal $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$ (leakage $\varepsilon$ small), the effective routing signal power is:
1004	\[
1005	    P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) \;=\; (1{-}\alpha)^2 \cdot [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] \;+\; \alpha^2 \cdot \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)} \;+\; 2\alpha(1{-}\alpha)\,\mathrm{Cov}_\mathrm{cross}
1006	\]
1007	Routing discriminability crosses the router's noise floor at a critical normalization threshold:
1008	\[
1009	    \alpha^* \;\approx\; \frac{R(\mathcal{D})}{R(\mathcal{D}) + 1}
1010	\]
1011	For $\alpha < \alpha^*$, routing quality degrades continuously; for $\alpha \to 1$, routing collapses discontinuously due to the softmax's exponential sensitivity to signal-to-noise ratio.
1012	\end{proposition}
1013	
1014	\emph{Validation.} For the median $R(\mathcal{D}) = 0.67$ across our benchmarks, Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition} predicts $\alpha^* \approx 0.40$. The dose-response experiment (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs) confirms this: MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha \leq 0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha = 1.0$ ($+283\%$). The sharpness of the transition arises from the softmax: when $P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) / P_\mathrm{noise}$ drops below ${\sim}1$, routing weights converge to uniform regardless of expert relevance.
1015	
1016	\textbf{Information bottleneck connection.}
1017	The RevIN-encoder pipeline implements a form of the information bottleneck~\citep{tishby2000ib}: it compresses $X$ into a representation $H = f_\theta(S)$ that is optimized for downstream prediction while discarding ``irrelevant'' variability (the per-window location-scale statistics). The routing MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) is the price paid for this compression \emph{at the routing decision point}. This connects to a broader principle: any architecture that bottlenecks information for one objective (prediction) can inadvertently destroy information needed for another (routing). The vision cross-modality control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) confirms this is not RevIN-specific: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patches creates the same bottleneck, while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does not---because spatial features are not the routing signal for classification.
1018

1019	\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}} (Gradient Co-Adaptation Drives Entropy Collapse).
1020	
1021	\begin{proof}
1022	Consider a single input $\mathbf{x}$ with backbone $\mathbf{h} = A\mathbf{x}$, router $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{h})$, and loss $\ell = p\,\ell_1(\mathbf{h}) + (1-p)\,\ell_2(\mathbf{h})$.
1023	
1024	\emph{Part (i): Unfrozen backbone.} The gradient with respect to $A$ is:
1025	\begin{equation*}
1026	\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial A} = p\,\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\mathbf{x}^\top + (1{-}p)\,\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\mathbf{x}^\top + (\ell_1 - \ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\,\mathbf{w}\mathbf{x}^\top
1027	\end{equation*}
1028	Under gradient descent $\dot{A} = -\eta\,\partial\ell/\partial A$, the induced change in expert~1's loss is:
1029	\begin{multline*}
1030	\dot{\ell}_1\big|_A = -\eta\|\mathbf{x}\|^2\!\Bigg[p\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2 + (1{-}p)\left(\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right)^{\!\top}\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}} \\
1031	 + (\ell_1{-}\ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\left(\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right)^{\!\top}\mathbf{w}\Bigg]
1032	\end{multline*}
1033	The first term (self-gradient) always decreases $\ell_1$. The second (cross-gradient) is negligible when expert gradients are approximately orthogonal---a condition that holds empirically once experts specialize to distinct input clusters (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_weights}). The third (loss-coupling) term is small early in training when $|\ell_1 - \ell_2| \ll \|\partial\ell_1/\partial\mathbf{h}\|$. Retaining only the dominant first term:
1034	\begin{equation*}
1035	\dot{\ell}_1\big|_A \approx -\eta\,p\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2
1036	\end{equation*}
1037	and analogously $\dot{\ell}_2\big|_A \approx -\eta\,(1{-}p)\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2$. When $p > 1{-}p$ (expert~1 dominates), $\ell_1$ decreases faster than $\ell_2$. The third term in $\partial\ell/\partial A$ further reinforces this: when $\ell_1 < \ell_2$, the factor $(\ell_1 - \ell_2) < 0$ drives $\dot{p} > 0$, pushing $p$ toward~1. Together these create the self-reinforcing loop: dominant expert gets more gradient $\to$ its loss drops faster $\to$ router increases its weight $\to$ it becomes more dominant.
1038	
1039	\emph{Part (ii): Frozen backbone.} When $A$ is fixed, $\dot{A} = 0$. The only dynamics are through $\mathbf{w}$:
1040	\begin{equation*}
1041	\dot{\mathbf{w}} = -\eta\,\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{w}} = -\eta\,(\ell_1 - \ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\,\mathbf{h}
1042	\end{equation*}
1043	This update adjusts routing weights based on current expert performance, but does \emph{not} reshape $\mathbf{h}$ to favor one expert. Without the $A$-mediated feedback loop, there is no systematic bias toward entropy collapse---the router converges to a stable allocation reflecting the static geometry of the fixed representation space.
1044	\end{proof}
1045	
1046	\section{AAS Search Details}
1047	\label{app:aas_details}
1048	
1049	The AAS loop maintains a population of 20 adapters over 12 generations (${\sim}240$ evaluations, 3-epoch fitness probes). Elitism preserves the top 2; an LLM variant generates candidates in the code space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$. Template-based generation achieves 100\% validity (vs.\ ${\sim}75\%$ for LLM).
1050	
1051	\subsubsection*{Template Grammar Production Rules}
1052	\label{app:grammar}
1053	
1054	\begin{align*}
1055	S &\rightarrow \nonterminal{Pool} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{MLP} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{Output} \\
1056	\nonterminal{Pool} &\rightarrow \text{MeanPool} \mid \text{MaxPool} \mid \text{LastToken} \mid \text{AttnPool} \mid \text{Conv1dPool} \\
1057	\nonterminal{MLP} &\rightarrow \nonterminal{Layer} \mid \nonterminal{Layer} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{MLP} \quad (\text{depth} \leq 3) \\
1058	\nonterminal{Layer} &\rightarrow \text{Linear}(d_\text{in}, d_\text{out}) \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{Act} \;\cdot\; \text{Dropout}(p) \\
1059	\nonterminal{Act} &\rightarrow \text{GELU} \mid \text{ReLU} \mid \text{SiLU} \mid \text{Tanh} \\
1060	\nonterminal{Output} &\rightarrow \text{Linear}(d_\text{last}, H)
1061	\end{align*}
1062	with $d_\text{out} \in \{64, 128, 192, 256, 384\}$ and $p \in \{0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$, yielding $|\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}| \approx 1{,}200$.

1125	\section{Formal Definitions}
1126	\label{app:formal_defs}
1127	
1128	\begin{definition}[Adapter]
1129	Given a pretrained TSFM backbone $f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{B \times L} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d}$ that maps input time series to encoder hidden states, an \textbf{adapter} is a parameterized module $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ that maps hidden states to forecasts, where $\phi \in \Phi_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n_g}$ are trainable weights with $n_g \leq N_\text{max}$ (we set $N_\text{max} = 500{,}000$).
1130	\end{definition}

1349	\textbf{What the router learns.} Per-sample routing decisions correlate with amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$), while Expert~2 (max-pool) handles low-amplitude windows and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude windows. The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the distribution tails, empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$ of Part~(iii) of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.
1350	
1351	\begin{figure}[h]
1352	\centering
1353	\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/routing_viz.pdf}
1354	\caption{\textbf{Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(iii).}
1355	\label{fig:routing_viz}
1356	\end{figure}
1357	
1358	\textbf{Regime-specific adaptation.} Partitioning test windows into quartiles by amplitude, RR-MoA wins \textbf{all four quartiles} across all 9 (dataset, seed) pairs, with the largest improvement on quiet, low-amplitude windows (Q1: $4.6{\times}$ better, $0.24$ vs $1.09$ on ETTh1) and the smallest on volatile, high-amplitude windows (Q4: $1.3{\times}$, $1.54$ vs $1.97$).
1359	
1360	\textbf{Sufficient statistic router (SSR).} A router using only $[\mu(X_\text{raw}), \sigma(X_\text{raw})]$---functionally equivalent to a DishTS-style~\citep{fan2023dishts} routing mechanism that conditions on the exact statistics distribution-shift methods re-inject---degrades MSE by $+48\%$ on average ($+11\%$ to $+94\%$) vs.\ the Conv1d router across all 8 forecasting datasets. The degradation is largest on ETTm2 ($+94\%$) and Exchange ($+82\%$), and smallest on Weather ($+11\%$). While Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of the information loss, effective routing requires temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale statistics.
1361	
1362	\textbf{Temporal-shuffle ablation.} We route on a fixed temporal permutation of $X_\text{raw}$---destroying time ordering while preserving distributional statistics ($M$, $\Sigma$, histogram shape). Across 6 datasets (frozen, 5 seeds), shuffled routing performs within ${\pm}3\%$ of raw routing on 4/6 datasets (ETTh1 $+3.2\%$, ETTh2 $+1.2\%$, ETTm1 $-1.2\%$, Electricity $+0.7\%$), with Weather improving $-8.5\%$ and ETTm2 improving $-16.0\%$. Entropy remains high ($1.43$--$1.58$). This confirms that the Conv1d router primarily extracts distributional rather than temporal features from $X_\text{raw}$. Combined with the SSR result ($+48\%$ degradation using only $[\mu, \sigma]$), the picture is: distributional statistics provide the \emph{essential} routing signal, but temporal shape (which the shuffle preserves as histogram features in the Conv1d) provides an additional ${\sim}10\%$ refinement.
1363	
1364	\textbf{Router-Detached Gradient Flow (RDGF).} A variant that unfreezes the backbone but replaces routing-weighted gradients with uniform-average gradients ($\nabla_H \mathcal{L}_\text{backbone} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_k \nabla_H \mathcal{L}_k$) degrades MSE by $+35\%$ to $+100\%$ across three datasets. This confirms the Frozen Paradox is structural.
1365	
1366	\textbf{Spectral-temporal router (FFT-Router).} We augment the Conv1d router with explicit frequency-domain features: a parallel branch applies rFFT to $X_\text{raw}$, extracts the top-32 spectral amplitudes, and concatenates them with the Conv1d temporal embedding before the routing head. On the two datasets with matched dense-frozen baselines, FFT-Router \emph{degrades} MSE by $+6\%$ (Weather) and $+22\%$ (ETTm1). The Conv1d router already captures frequency-relevant patterns implicitly; adding explicit spectral features overparameterizes the router without improving routing quality.
1367	
1368	\textbf{Statistic-aware information bottleneck (SAIB).} An auxiliary loss forces the router's penultimate representation to predict the window-level $[\mu, \sigma]$---directly operationalizing Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. With SAIB coefficients $\lambda \in \{0.1, 1.0\}$, MSE is unchanged on ETTm1 ($0.395$ vs $0.397$ baseline) and slightly degraded on Weather ($0.250$ vs $0.236$). Routing entropy increases to $1.55$ (near-maximum $\log 5 = 1.61$), indicating the auxiliary loss disperses routing weights without improving forecast accuracy. This confirms the Conv1d router already encodes $\mu, \sigma$ without explicit supervision.
1369	
1370	\textbf{Instance-adaptive gating (IA-Gating).} In the dual-stream variant (Appendix~\ref{app:gap_closing}), we replace the static per-expert blending scalar $\alpha$ with a per-window gate $\gamma(X_\text{raw}) = \sigma(W_g \cdot z)$ where $z$ is the router's latent representation. Across 6 datasets (frozen, 3 seeds), IA-Gating wins on 4/6 (ETTh2 $-8.0\%$, ETTm2 $-6.4\%$, ETTm1 $-1.9\%$, Electricity $-0.4\%$) and loses on 2/6 (Weather $+6.1\%$, ETTh1 $+0.3\%$). The learned gates cluster tightly around $\gamma \approx 0.48$ across all datasets and windows, indicating the backbone's contribution is roughly constant per-window---which explains why the simpler static $\alpha$ performs comparably overall.
1371	
1372	\subsection{Statistics Re-Injection Ablation}
1373	\label{app:reinjection}
1374	
1375	A natural counter to RR-MoA is: ``why not re-inject the stripped statistics into the hidden states rather than routing on the full raw signal?'' We test this by replacing the raw-input router with a \emph{hidden-reinjected} router: the gate receives $[\text{mean-pool}(\mathbf{H});\, \mu(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \sigma(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})]$ (a $d{+}2$-dimensional vector) instead of $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$.

Two scalars grafted onto a $512$-dim homogenized representation are insufficient to recover routing signal.}

This confirms that the raw signal carries routing information beyond the two-scalar $(\mu,\sigma)$ summary, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+48\%$ degradation from the full Conv1d router; \S\ref{app:routing_ablations}). 1491	\subsection{AdaMix Implementation Details}
1492	\label{app:adamix_details}
1493	
1494	Our AdaMix baseline follows \citet{wang2022adamix} with $K{=}5$ expert adapter heads identical to RR-MoA's canonical pool (mean, last, max, attention, conv1d). The router is a single linear layer $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^K$ operating on the mean-pooled hidden state, with softmax gating. We use a load-balancing auxiliary loss with coefficient $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$, matching AdaMix's original formulation. No stochastic routing, capacity factors, or noise injection are applied---these standard MoE safeguards do not address the normalization-specific signal loss we identify: when RevIN strips the per-window statistics that would distinguish samples, the router receives near-identical inputs regardless of stabilization strategy. This is confirmed empirically: load-balancing loss does not prevent collapse under unfreezing (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, entropy $= 0.000$ with $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$), while disabling RevIN recovers entropy to $0.66$--$1.32$ without any routing regularization.

Table~\ref{tab:adamix_raw} shows results across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds (36 runs).

1545	\label{app:norm_generalization}

1547	To test whether routing collapse is specific to RevIN or a general property of instance-level normalization, we replace MOMENT's RevIN with two alternative normalizers---BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm (1 group)---and run AdaMix with last-4 unfreezing on ETTh1.

1557	\midrule

1566	
1567	All three normalizers cause entropy collapse to ${\leq}0.004$, while removing normalization entirely keeps entropy stable at $0.817$. The mechanism is the same in each case: the normalizer strips per-window statistics before the encoder, the router receives homogenized hidden states, and gradient co-adaptation amplifies the initial routing bias into full collapse. This confirms that the normalization-routing tension is a \emph{general} property of instance-level normalization, not a RevIN-specific artifact. Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts that collapse occurs specifically when the stripped statistics carry routing signal; a cross-modality control on ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) validates this: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$), while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does \emph{not}---exactly as the theory predicts.

1594	\textbf{ResNet-18: normalization prevents collapse.} Without normalization (C), the unfrozen backbone co-adapts with the dominant expert, collapsing entropy to $0.184\pm0.260$---confirming Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}. Adding InstanceNorm2d (A) or BatchNorm2d (D) \emph{prevents} collapse ($1.48\pm0.02$), the \emph{opposite} of time series. Why: InstanceNorm2d strips per-channel spatial mean/variance, which carry negligible routing information for image classification (analogous to Traffic, $R{=}0.14$).
1595	
1596	\textbf{ViT-B/16: normalization causes collapse.} Extending to a Vision Transformer, InstanceNorm1d on frozen ViT patch embeddings collapses routing to $0.000\pm0.000$ (E), while the same backbone without normalization maintains healthy routing at $0.494\pm0.130$ (F). InstanceNorm1d normalizes per-channel across the 197-token sequence, stripping per-patch mean/scale statistics---structurally identical to RevIN on time-series windows. The routing signal in ViT resides partly in patch-level statistics (which patches are bright, high-contrast, textured), so stripping them degrades the router.

1645	
1646	On ETTh1 and ETTm1, identical pools degrade by $10$--$29\%$ (except Conv1d on ETTh1, which matches). On Weather, identical pools paradoxically improve by $9$--$16\%$. This suggests that on low-complexity datasets, inductive-bias homogeneity can reduce interference, while on higher-complexity datasets, architectural diversity provides complementary representations the router can exploit. The canonical diverse pool is the safer default across the full benchmark.

The mechanism is identical: RevIN strips the hidden-state heterogeneity regardless of whether the expert head predicts a forecast or reconstructs masked values.

1700	\section{Learnable Normalization Coefficient}
1701	\label{app:learnable_alpha}
1702	
1703	To test whether gradient descent independently discovers Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}'s prediction, we parameterize the router input as $\mathbf{r} = \sigma(\ell)\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{X}) + (1 - \sigma(\ell))\,\mathbf{X}_{\text{raw}}$, where $\ell$ is a scalar \texttt{nn.Parameter} initialized to $0$ (so $\alpha = \sigma(0) = 0.5$). All other settings match the standard RR-MoA config (MOMENT-small, frozen, Top-2, $K{=}5$, $H{=}96$, 15 epochs).

1724	All 30 runs converge to $\alpha < 0.5$ (range $0.445$--$0.491$), with trajectories monotonically decreasing from the $0.492$ initialization. The unanimity is the key finding: gradient descent independently discovers that raw input carries more routing information, confirming the qualitative prediction of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. The narrow converged range ($0.459$--$0.482$) means the magnitude does not strongly differentiate datasets---the signal is binary (raw $>$ norm), not graded.

1726	\section{Exact MI Loss and Bound Tightness}
1727	\label{app:mi_tightness}
1728	
1729	Since the router is deterministic ($E = \arg\max$), $I(X;E) = H(E)$ and the exact MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) reduces to $H(E \mid S)$. We estimate this directly: train the RR-MoA router on raw windows, extract expert assignments $E$, then train an MLP classifier ($512 \to 256 \to 128 \to K$) to predict $E$ from the RevIN-normalized shape $S$. The held-out cross-entropy (temperature-calibrated) gives $H(E \mid S)$.
1730	
1731	\begin{table}[h]
1732	\centering
1733	\caption{\textbf{Exact MI loss measurement and bound tightness} (3 seeds). $H(E \mid S)$ is the exact routing information lost to normalization. Retention $= I(S;E)/H(E)$. LB = lower bound from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii). Gap $= I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ via within-expert CCA.}
1734	\label{tab:mi_tightness}
1735	\small
1736	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccr@{}}
1737	\toprule
1738	Dataset & $H(E)$ & $H(E \mid S)$ & Ret\% & LB & Gap & $\Delta\%$ \\
1739	\midrule
1740	ETTh1       & 0.73 & 0.61 & 16.3 & 0.02 & 0.06 & $-43.2$ \\
1741	ETTh2       & 0.76 & 0.57 & 26.3 & 0.00 & 0.10 & $-71.0$ \\
1742	ETTm1       & 0.75 & 0.57 & 24.2 & 0.18 & 0.03 & $-51.1$ \\
1743	ETTm2       & 0.82 & 0.53 & 35.1 & 0.18 & 0.07 & $-77.2$ \\
1744	Weather     & 1.37 & 0.98 & 29.1 & 0.61 & 0.08 & $-44.6$ \\
1745	Electricity & 0.68 & 0.46 & 32.4 & 0.13 & 0.02 & $-26.8$ \\
1746	Traffic     & 0.63 & 0.44 & 24.6 & 0.19 & 0.02 & $+2.9$ \\
1747	Exchange    & 0.63 & 0.44 & 22.1 & 0.00 & 0.10 & $-66.5$ \\
1748	Solar       & 0.97 & 0.57 & 40.9 & 0.08 & 0.20 & $-32.9$ \\
1749	\bottomrule
1750	\end{tabular}
1751	\end{table}
1752	
1753	\textbf{Key findings.} (1)~Normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy across all nine datasets, confirming that RevIN universally degrades routing signal. (2)~The bound gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$), so the lower bound is empirically tight. (3)~Crucially, $H(E \mid S)$ does \emph{not} correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$, $p{=}0.77$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$). This distinction is informative: $H(E \mid S)$ measures how much routing information the \emph{specific trained router} loses, while $R(\mathcal{D})$ measures the \emph{potential} routing information that location-scale statistics could carry. The gap between these explains why some datasets with low MI loss still benefit substantially from raw routing---the router adapts to use whatever signal remains, but the \emph{quality} of that signal (captured by $R$) determines downstream task performance.
1754	
1755	\textbf{Synthetic validation.} On Gaussian mixture data ($K{=}5$ clusters) with analytically known MI, we sweep the shape-statistics correlation $\rho_{MS} \in [0, 0.9]$. At $\rho_{MS}{=}0$, the bound is tight (gap $= 0.19$ nats, $12\%$ of $\log K$). As $\rho_{MS}$ increases, the bound becomes vacuous ($\varepsilon$ exceeds $I(M,\Sigma;E)$), but $H(E \mid S)$ remains informative throughout---validating our direct measurement approach.

1799	Residual correction experiments further confirm that backbone features provide negligible complementary signal: adding backbone features (via Ridge or Random Forest) as a residual correction atop a linear raw-input predictor improves MSE by at most $0.55\%$. On ETTh1, Random Forest regression on raw input alone reduces MSE by $44\%$ versus Ridge, revealing substantial nonlinear temporal structure in the raw data. However, Random Forest on backbone features adds only $+0.02\%$ to the linear baseline---the encoder destroys this nonlinear structure entirely. Few-shot experiments (Table~\ref{tab:fewshot}) confirm the pattern holds at every training set size $N \in \{10, \ldots, 5000\}$: DLinear dominates at all $N$, ruling out data scarcity as a regime where the frozen backbone recovers its advantage. The gap to DLinear reflects information destruction by the normalization--encoding pipeline, not a limitation of adapter design or training data volume.

1911	\section{Deployment-Regime Motivation}
1912	\label{app:deployment}
1913	
1914	The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
1915	
1916	\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Per-tenant DLinear requires collecting, storing, and periodically retraining on each tenant's historical data ($O(N)$ training pipelines for $N$ tenants), whereas the frozen backbone is loaded once and adapter weights (${\sim}50$--$500$K parameters, ${\sim}0.2$--$2$\,MB) are swapped from host RAM in microseconds. At $N{=}1{,}000$ tenants, the adapter approach eliminates $1{,}000$ independent training jobs and enables instant onboarding of new tenants via zero-shot transfer---capabilities absent from per-tenant supervised baselines.
1917	
1918	\textbf{(ii) On-device and edge deployment.} One backbone is shipped with the device image; per-site adapters are updated over low-bandwidth links. Collecting each site's training data centrally is often impossible for privacy or latency reasons.
1919	
1920	\textbf{(iii) Cross-task reuse.} The same frozen backbone drives forecasting, imputation, and classification via different expert pools. We demonstrate the first two tasks explicitly in the main text.
1921

1942	
1943	The RR-MoA routing overhead ($+4.3$\,ms) is dominated by the sparse expert selection loop; the router itself (Conv1d + linear, ${\sim}1.1$K params) adds $<0.1$\,ms. At deployment scale, adapter swapping between tenants requires loading $426$K parameters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB) from host RAM---orders of magnitude cheaper than reloading a $35$M parameter backbone. At $N{=}100$ tenants, adapter-swapping throughput is $141$ tenants/sec. The memory footprint of a shared-backbone deployment ($1\times$ TSFM at $140$\,MB plus $100\times$ RR-MoA adapters at $1.7$\,MB each $= 310$\,MB total) is $45\times$ smaller than naively replicating the full backbone per tenant ($100 \times 140$\,MB $= 14\,000$\,MB). \textbf{Honest caveat:} this $45\times$ figure is against the naive per-tenant-TSFM baseline, which no rational deployer would run; against per-tenant DLinear ($100 \times 49$K parameters $= 19.6$\,MB total) the shared-TSFM approach is roughly $15\times$ \emph{larger}, not smaller. The memory argument for TSFMs over DLinear is therefore not the core motivation --- that role is played by cross-task reuse, zero-shot onboarding, and the elimination of $O(N)$ per-tenant training pipelines (see \S\ref{sec:intro} and Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}).

1945	\section{Extended Full Fine-Tuning Ablation}
1946	\label{app:extended_ft}
1947	
1948	To rule out optimization confounds in the Frozen Paradox, we extend full fine-tuning from the standard 15-epoch Adam protocol to stronger schedules: 50 epochs, cosine LR with 3-epoch warmup, layer-wise LR decay ($\gamma{=}0.8$), and AdamW with weight decay $0.01$.

1972	
1973	The best extended schedule (50ep cosine + layer-wise LR decay) improves over the 15-epoch baseline by only $4$--$5\%$, while frozen RR-MoA maintains a $33$--$41\%$ advantage. \textbf{Stronger optimization does not help.} We additionally swept 10 aggressive configurations at 100 epochs with $\text{lr}{\in}\{10^{-5}, 10^{-6}\}$, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay ($\gamma{=}0.8$), weight decay ${\in}\{0.001, 0.01, 0.1\}$, gradient accumulation (effective batch 256/512), and gradient clipping ($\|g\|_2 {\leq} 1.0$) --- 90 total configurations across 3 datasets $\times$ 3 seeds. The best per-dataset results (ETTh1: $1.030$, ETTm1: $0.877$, Weather: $0.471$) are \emph{worse} than the 50-epoch reference, confirming the Frozen Paradox is not an optimization artifact. The gap to frozen RR-MoA remains $51$--$71\%$.
1974	
1975	\textbf{Causal proof via RevIN ablation.} Disabling RevIN inside MOMENT dramatically recovers full-FT performance: ETTh1 ($1.063 \to 0.490$, $-54\%$), ETTm1 ($0.910 \to 0.364$, $-60\%$), Weather ($0.481 \to 0.187$, $-61\%$). With RevIN disabled, full-FT matches or exceeds supervised baselines---confirming that RevIN, not the optimization protocol, is the root cause of the paradox.
1976	
1977	\textbf{Adapter training budget.} Extending adapter-only training (frozen backbone) from 15 to 50 epochs improves RR-MoA by $8$--$14\%$: ETTh1 ($0.690 \to 0.633$), ETTm1 ($0.572 \to 0.494$), Weather ($0.289 \to 0.250$). This narrows the supervised gap modestly but does not close it, consistent with the representation-bottleneck diagnosis: additional adapter training cannot recover information the backbone's normalization discarded. The remaining gap reflects the information ceiling of frozen backbone representations, not insufficient optimization of the adapter.
1978	
1979	\section{Closing the DLinear Gap}
1980	\label{app:gap_closing}
1981	\label{app:gap_closing_ext}
1982	
1983	A good diagnosis should be \emph{actionable}: identifying the root cause of a performance gap should point directly to how to close it. Our diagnosis pinpoints the DLinear gap as information destruction by the normalization--encoding pipeline (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}): experts operate on hidden states from which RevIN and patching have stripped fine-grained temporal structure. This diagnosis makes a clear architectural prediction: \emph{if we restore raw-signal access to the experts, the gap should close.} We test this prediction with three architectures.
1984	
1985	We test three architectures that provide experts with raw-input access while preserving the frozen-backbone paradigm and RR-MoA routing:
1986	
1987	\textbf{(1)~Dual-Stream.} Each expert blends a backbone branch (existing adapter head on $\mathbf{H}$) with a raw branch (MLP on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$) via a learnable per-expert scalar $\alpha_k$: $\mathbf{y}_k = \sigma(\alpha_k)\cdot\text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H}) + (1{-}\sigma(\alpha_k))\cdot\text{MLP}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$.
1988	
1989	\textbf{(2)~Raw-Input Expert.} A 6th expert operating directly on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ (bypassing the backbone) is added to the pool; the router decides per-sample whether to use backbone-based or raw-input experts.
1990	
1991	\textbf{(3)~Multi-Resolution.} Each expert concatenates projected raw features with pooled hidden-state features before forecasting: $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{MLP}([\text{Proj}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \text{Pool}_k(\mathbf{H})])$.
1992	
1993	\begin{table}[h]
1994	\centering
1995	\caption{\textbf{Closing the DLinear gap} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds, H=96). Dual-stream experts that access both hidden states and raw input narrow the gap from $+33$--$75\%$ to $+9$--$11\%$ and \textbf{beat DLinear on Weather}. Learned $\alpha{\approx}0.49$ confirms the backbone contributes complementary information when combined with raw access.}
1996	\label{tab:gap_closing}

2011	
2012	\textbf{Result.} Dual-stream experts reduce the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5\%$---an $11\times$ reduction---and \emph{beat} DLinear on Weather ($0.198$ vs $0.208$, $p{=}0.03$, paired $t$-test). The learned blend parameters $\alpha_k \approx 0.49$ across all five experts confirm that the backbone provides complementary information when experts can also access the raw signal: neither branch alone suffices.
2013	
2014	\textbf{Extension to ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity.} Running all four variants on the three remaining forecasting datasets yields consistent gap closure (Table~\ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}). Dual-stream wins on Electricity at $+8\%$ and matches well on ETTm2 ($+26\%$), while \textbf{multi-resolution wins on ETTh2 at $+7.7\%$}---the tightest new gap-closing result on any dataset we did not originally study. Multi-resolution also performs competitively on ETTm2 ($+12\%$) and Electricity ($+13\%$), indicating the optimal architecture is dataset-dependent. FiLM remains consistently worst ($+48$--$147\%$), confirming that re-injecting only $(\mu,\sigma)$ is insufficient---the experts need access to the full raw signal, not just the stripped statistics.

2034	
2035	\textbf{Why this matters for the diagnosis.} The fact that the gap closes precisely when experts recover the information our diagnosis identified as destroyed---and remains open when they cannot (FiLM re-injects only $\mu,\sigma$, yielding $+48\%$ on ETTh1 vs.\ $+9\%$ for dual-stream)---is direct evidence that the diagnosis is both \emph{correct} and \emph{actionable}. The normalization--encoding bottleneck is not merely an observation; it is the causal mechanism whose resolution closes the gap. Importantly, the frozen backbone and raw-routed paradigm remain unchanged---these variants extend the \emph{expert architecture}, not the routing mechanism, confirming that the routing diagnosis (the core contribution of this paper) is orthogonal to expert design.
2036	
2037	\textbf{Expert pool ablation: canonical vs.\ macro pool.} To test whether RR-MoA's benefits depend on the specific choice of 5 canonical pooling heads, we replace the canonical pool with 5 AAS-discovered \emph{macro motifs} (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}) and rerun RR-MoA across all 6 forecasting datasets. Routing entropy is preserved under the macro pool (no collapse under frozen backbone; entropy $>1.3$ across all configurations), confirming that the collapse-prevention mechanism is \emph{pool-independent}. Absolute MSEs (frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds): ETTh1 $0.764{\pm}0.015$, ETTh2 $0.667{\pm}0.069$, ETTm1 $0.583{\pm}0.075$, ETTm2 $0.844{\pm}0.241$, Weather $0.274{\pm}0.024$, Electricity $0.401{\pm}0.039$. The canonical pool is stronger by $8$--$24\%$ on the three datasets where we have both numbers, indicating that while RR-MoA generalizes across diverse pool designs, the canonical heads are better tuned for the forecasting benchmark---the routing architecture is the orthogonal contribution.
2038	
2039	\textbf{Training-length ablation.} We additionally ran dual-stream at 50 epochs (vs.\ 15 in Table~\ref{tab:gap_closing}). Extended training \emph{overfits} on 5/6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.453{\to}0.556$; Weather: $0.198{\to}0.237$), confirming that dual-stream converges by 15 epochs and that the original training schedule is already near-optimal; additional adapter-only optimization past convergence degrades generalization due to the small effective parameter count ($\sim$718K trainable, frozen backbone).

2173	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit{Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit{Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma$ gates (orange) on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf{6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf{107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times$ 6 datasets $\times$ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}
2174	\label{fig:residual_ia_arch}
2175	\end{figure}
2176	
2177	The dual-stream and multi-resolution variants narrow the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5$--$8\%$ (Tables~\ref{tab:gap_closing}, \ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}) but win on only 1/6 datasets (Weather). A systematic $546$-run hyperparameter sweep uncovered a \emph{second} hidden pathology and the architectural fix that closes the remaining gap to \textbf{4/6 match-or-beat}.
2178	
2179	\textbf{Diagnostic: gates fail to learn.} We instrumented the per-sample gate mechanism to log its mean activation per expert per dataset. Across every configuration tested---\{rh128, rh192, rh256, rh320, rh384, rh512\} $\times$ \{d1, d2, d3 raw-branch depth\} $\times$ \{lr, wd, cosine, warmup\} hyperparameter combinations---the learned gates consistently plateau at $\sigma(0.0){\approx}0.5$:
2180	
2181	\begin{center}
2182	\small
2183	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc@{}}
2184	\toprule
2185	Config & ETTh1 & ETTh2 & ETTm1 & ETTm2 & Weather & Elec. \\
2186	\midrule
2187	Dual-stream ($\alpha_k$)             & $0.49$ & $0.50$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ \\
2188	Residual-IA (gate-init $b{=}0$)      & $0.47$ & $0.50$ & $0.48$ & $0.49$ & $0.49$ & $0.47$ \\
2189	Residual-IA + cos+wd ($b{=}0$)       & $0.50$ & $0.51$ & $0.49$ & $0.52$ & $0.50$ & $0.49$ \\
2190	\bottomrule
2191	\end{tabular}
2192	\end{center}
2193	
2194	With 15 epochs of training, the gate mechanism extracts no gradient signal about \emph{which branch should dominate} because both branches receive co-equal credit for reducing loss from the start. This is isomorphic to the dual-stream $\alpha_k \approx 0.49$ observation, indicating it is not a quirk of a single architecture but a general failure mode of symmetrically-initialized mixture mechanisms on this task.
2195	
2196	\textbf{Three surgical fixes.}
2197	(i)~\textbf{Residual formulation.} Re-express the expert as $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{Raw}_k(\mathbf{X}) + g_k(\mathbf{X})\cdot\text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, making the raw branch the \emph{primary predictor} and the backbone an additive residual that must earn its contribution.
2198	(ii)~\textbf{Gate-init bias $b{=}{-}2$.} Initialize the gate-head linear layer's bias at $-2$ so that $g_k \approx \sigma({-}2){=}0.12$ at epoch~$0$: the backbone contributes only $12\%$ initially. The model is \emph{essentially DLinear at initialization} and the backbone must earn any opening of the gate.
2199	(iii)~\textbf{$5$-epoch raw-branch warmup.} For epochs $1$--$5$, freeze both the backbone branch and the gate head so only the raw branch and router train. The raw branch converges to a DLinear-quality base predictor; then at epoch~$6$ the backbone+gate unfreeze and must add value as a residual on top of an already-good base.
2200	
2201	We additionally simplify the raw branch to a single linear layer ($\text{Linear}(512{\to}96)$, ``$d1$'')---which is structurally identical to DLinear---and add cosine LR decay with weight decay $10^{-4}$ for stable long-horizon training.
2202	
2203	\begin{table}[h]
2204	\centering
2205	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA (intermediate)} (MOMENT-small, frozen, Top-2, H=96; Welch $t$-test vs.\ DLinear). Achieves \textbf{4/6 match-or-beat}: one sig win (Weather), one mean win (ETTm2), two parity, two sig losses. Avg gap $+1.6\%$. Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus} shows the improved Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} (5/6).}
2206	\label{tab:residual_ia}

2223	
2224	\textbf{Why it works mechanistically.} The symmetric $\sigma(0){=}0.5$ initialization treats the two branches as a priori equally reliable. For LTSF benchmarks where the raw signal contains most of the predictive structure (DLinear's success is evidence of this), this prior is wrong. The asymmetric $b{=}{-}2$ initialization encodes the correct inductive bias: \emph{``default to a linear projection of the raw signal; invoke the backbone only if it reduces the loss.''} The $5$-epoch warmup separates the learning phases: the raw branch does not have to compete with a half-trained backbone for the same gradient signal during the critical early epochs. Each fix alone yields only marginal gains (see below); only their combination achieves $4/6$ match-or-beat.
2225	
2226	\textbf{Ablation: which fix does how much?} We isolate the contribution of each intervention (each row $n{=}3$ seeds, otherwise identical to Residual-IA):
2227	
2228	\begin{center}
2229	\footnotesize
2230	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc|c@{}}
2231	\toprule
2232	Variant & ETTh1 & ETTh2 & ETTm1 & ETTm2 & Weather & Elec. & Wins \\
2233	\midrule
2234	Dual-stream (baseline)       & $0.453$ & $0.452$ & $0.358$ & $0.252$ & $\mathbf{0.198}$ & $0.171$ & $1$ \\
2235	+ residual + IA gate ($b{=}0$) & $0.505$ & $0.520$ & $0.393$ & $0.231$ & $0.210$ & $0.170$ & $0$ \\
2236	+ cos + wd ($b{=}0$)         & $0.460$ & $0.398$ & $0.348$ & $\mathbf{0.194}$ & $0.190$ & $0.163$ & $2$ \\
2237	+ linear raw ($b{=}0$)  & $0.436$ & $0.375$ & $0.325$ & $0.202$ & $0.193$ & $0.160$ & $1$\textsuperscript{$\star$} \\
2238	+ $b{=}{-}2$                 & $0.432$ & $0.388$ & $0.331$ & $0.224$ & $0.191$ & $0.160$ & $1$\textsuperscript{$\star$} \\
2239	\textbf{+ warmup $=5$ (final)} & $\mathbf{0.437}$ & $\mathbf{0.382}$ & $\mathbf{0.327}$ & $0.195$ & $0.193$ & $\mathbf{0.160}$ & $\mathbf{4}$ \\
2240	\bottomrule
2241	\end{tabular}
2242	\end{center}
2243	{\scriptsize $^{\star}$Column ``Wins'' counts datasets where mean MSE $<$ DLinear; parity (gap ${<}2\%$, $p{>}0.2$) counted separately above.}
2244	
2245	Each of the three fixes alone produces $0$--$2$ wins; only their combination produces $2$ wins + $2$ statistical-parity + $1$ marginal = $4/6$ match-or-beat. This is consistent with the mechanistic explanation: the residual formulation, the asymmetric initialization, and the warmup are all solving the same root-cause problem (symmetric gradient competition between branches) from complementary angles.
2246	
2247	\subsubsection*{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}: closing the remaining gap to 5/6}
2248	
2249	\paragraph{Design methodology: hypothesis-driven decomposition.} Residual-IA leaves two statistically significant losses: ETTh1 ($+5.1\%$, $p{<}0.001$) and ETTh2 ($+10.6\%$, $p{=}0.019$). Two competing hypotheses could explain them:
2250	
2251	\begin{itemize}
2252	\item \textbf{H1 (data scarcity).} ETTh1/ETTh2 have $8{,}640$ raw samples each versus $34{,}560$ for ETTm*, and \texttt{max\_samples$=$5000} caps the adapter training set at $\approx 9\%$ of available windows for ETTh but $\approx 2\%$ for ETTm. The ETTh pair may be overly exposed to sampling noise.
2253	\item \textbf{H2 (parameter scarcity).} Residual-IA's $K{=}5$ independent raw branches total $245{,}760$ parameters ($5{\times}$ DLinear's $49{,}152$). On a $5{,}000$-window training set, this capacity excess could induce overfitting.
2254	\end{itemize}
2255	
2256	The two hypotheses make opposite interventions: H1 predicts that \emph{more data} (raising \texttt{max\_samples} to $100{,}000$) closes the gap; H2 predicts that \emph{fewer parameters} (sharing the raw branch across experts to reach DLinear's $49$K budget) closes it. We ran both as single-lever experiments in parallel (Batches~1a and~1b, $5$ seeds each).
2257	
2258	\textbf{Phase~1 --- hypothesis falsification.}
2259	\emph{Cap removal fails.} At \texttt{max\_samples$=$100000}, the ETTh2 gap widens from $+10.6\%$ to $+26\%$. The additional training data at the same $15$-epoch, lr${=}10^{-3}$, wd${=}10^{-4}$ recipe produces $11{\times}$ more update steps, over-regularizing through weight decay and preventing cosine-schedule convergence. This rules out H1.
2260	\emph{Shared raw branch succeeds.} At $K{=}5$ sharing a single $\text{Linear}(512, 96)$ module, raw parameters drop from $245$K to $49$K, exactly matching DLinear's budget. ETTh1 closes from $+5.1\%$ (sig loss) to $+1.6\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.086$); ETTh2 closes from $+10.6\%$ (sig loss) to $+7.0\%$ (marginal, $p{=}0.078$). Per-sample gates and distinct backbone branches remain per-expert, so expert specialization is preserved in \emph{how} the backbone residual is invoked---only the DLinear-equivalent base predictor is shared. The co-occurrence of H1's failure and H2's success identifies parameter bloat, not data scarcity, as the root cause.
2261	
2262	Phase~1 resolves the architectural pathology but leaves ETTh1/ETTh2 still marginally above DLinear. Phase~2 tests two orthogonal refinements motivated by properties specific to these datasets.
2263	
2264	\textbf{Phase~2 --- orthogonal refinements.}
2265	\emph{Non-stationarity (Batch~4).} Hourly ETT data exhibits pronounced per-window level drift---the train/test windows have different means. Standard LTSF practice addresses this with NLinear: $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$, where $x_T$ is a gradient-free anchor (the last input value). The linear layer is thereby constrained to model \emph{relative motion}, not absolute level. Testing \texttt{--raw-arch nlinear} as a drop-in replacement reduces ETTh1 from $+5.1\%$ to $+3.3\%$ and ETTh2 from $+10.6\%$ to $+6.9\%$ at $n{=}3$ seeds, while \emph{improving} (not regressing) ETTm2 ($-1.6\% \to -4.1\%$) and Weather ($-6.6\% \to -8.7\%$). The improvement is largest where non-stationarity is most pronounced, as expected.
2266	\emph{Per-dataset epoch mismatch (Batch~2).} A fixed $15$-epoch schedule assumes all datasets converge at the same rate. We test this by running validation-based early stopping with patience $5$ and logging the best epoch per seed. The result is striking: ETTh1 converges at epoch $7.2{\pm}1.2$, ETTh2 at $8.6{\pm}2.8$, ETTm1 at $14.8{\pm}3.7$, Weather at $8.6{\pm}1.2$, Electricity at $20.2{\pm}4.0$. No single fixed budget fits all six datasets---the $15$-epoch schedule simultaneously over-fits the ETTh pair and under-fits Electricity by $5$--$10$ epochs. Val-based early stopping (with gradient clipping at $\lVert g \rVert_2 \leq 1.0$ to stabilize the first epoch) achieves dataset-adaptive budgets without per-dataset hyperparameter tuning. In isolation this drops Electricity from $+0.6\%$ to $0.0\%$ (perfect parity, $p{=}0.991$) and Weather from $-6.6\%$ to $-4.6\%$ (nearing significance).
2267	
2268	\textbf{Phase~3 --- stacking validation.}
2269	Each Phase~1 and Phase~2 lever alone achieves only $3/6$--$4/6$ match-or-beat: shared raw closes ETTh1/h2 but trades small regressions on ETTm2; NLinear improves the ETTh pair but regresses ETTm1; val-early-stop perfects Electricity but hurts the ETTh pair by stopping too early. Each targets a different failure mode (parameter bloat, non-stationarity, training-length mismatch), and each mode is present on a different subset of the benchmark. \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} stacks all three:
2270	
2271	\begin{itemize}
2272	\item \textbf{(iv)}~\emph{Shared raw branch} --- single $\text{Linear}(512, 96)$ shared across $K$ experts.
2273	\item \textbf{(v)}~\emph{NLinear raw architecture} --- $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$.
2274	\item \textbf{(vi)}~\emph{Validation-based early stopping} --- patience $5$, gradient clipping $\lVert g \rVert_2 \leq 1.0$.
2275	\end{itemize}
2276	
2277	Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus} reports the composed result: $5/6$ match-or-beat at $-1.4\%$ mean gap (net win on average), with the fully-consistent per-dataset breakdown that each lever predicted in isolation.
2278	
2279	\begin{table}[h]
2280	\centering
2281	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}: final six-dataset gap-closing result at H${=}96$} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, $n{=}10$ seeds for both Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} \emph{and} DLinear; Welch two-sided $t$-test). Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} achieves \textbf{5/6 match-or-beat} with \textbf{three significant wins} ($p{\leq}0.002$): ETTm2 ($-10.8\%$, $p{=}0.002$), Weather ($-5.1\%$, $p{<}0.001$), Electricity ($-1.7\%$, $p{=}0.002$); one mean win (ETTh2 $-1.6\%$); one parity (ETTm1 $+0.4\%$, $p{=}0.68$); ETTh1 alone remains $+2.2\%$ ($p{=}0.037$). Mean gap: $\mathbf{-2.8\%}$ (net win).}

2319	\textbf{Why ETTh1 remains $+2.2\%$ at H${=}96$.} At $n{=}10$ for both methods, the ETTh1 gap is statistically significant ($p{=}0.037$), although the mean absolute MSE difference is only $0.009$ ($0.428$ vs.\ $0.419$). ETTh1 is the smallest LTSF dataset ($8{,}640$ raw samples), and its channels have strongly correlated seasonal patterns that a from-scratch linear model memorizes efficiently. At H${=}192$ the gap closes to \textbf{parity} ($+1.6\%$, $p{=}0.18$), consistent with DLinear's advantage being specific to short-horizon seasonal memorization on this dataset.

2321	\textbf{Implication.} Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} achieves \textbf{$107/123$ match-or-beat} ($88\%$) across six backbones, six datasets, and four horizons ($20/24$ MOMENT-small, $87/99$ cross-backbone; Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}), with $65$ significant wins vs $11$ losses ($5.9{:}1$ ratio) and \textbf{6/6 at H${=}192$}. MOMENT-large reaches $23/24$ ($96\%$); Moirai-MoE achieves $15/15$ with $-9.4\%$ mean gap, confirming adapter-level routing stacks with backbone-internal MoE. Practitioners requiring a shared-TSFM deployment topology (Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}) now have an adapter that matches or beats per-tenant DLinear on $100\%$ of benchmarks at H${=}192$.
2322	
2323	\subsubsection*{Multi-horizon generalization: H${\in}\{96, 192, 336, 720\}$}
2324	
2325	The Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} result above is computed at H${=}96$. We extend to the full set of standard LTSF horizons to verify the result is not horizon-specific. 2426	\subsection{SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+}: Self-Routed Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}}
2427	\label{app:sr_ria}
2428	
2429	SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+} combines two independently validated components: (i)~SR-MoA self-routing, where each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input (no external router; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}), and (ii)~Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}'s dual-stream expert architecture (shared NLinear raw branch + gated backbone residual; Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}). Each expert $k$ produces $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, where the NLinear branch is shared across experts and the blend gate is initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ ($\sigma(-2){\approx}0.12$). Training uses 5-epoch raw-branch warmup, cosine LR decay, and validation-based early stopping with patience 5.

2452	\subsection{Pure Raw-MLP MoE Ablation: How Much Does the TSFM Actually Contribute?}
2453	\label{app:raw_mlp_moe}
2454	
2455	A natural concern about the dual-stream gap-closing result is that it could be confounded: if the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure (Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}), and the dual-stream fix recovers that structure via the raw branch, perhaps the raw branch is doing all the work and the TSFM is dead weight. We tested this hypothesis directly by running a pure mixture-of-experts ablation in which the TSFM is removed entirely.
2456	
2457	\textbf{Architecture (E1, this work).} The Pure Raw-MLP MoE consists of $K{=}5$ size-diverse two-layer MLPs operating directly on the $512$-dimensional raw input window: hidden widths $\{64, 96, 128, 192, 256\}$ chosen so that the total parameter count ($449{,}557$) matches RR-MoA's $426$K within $5\%$. Each expert is $\text{Linear}(512{\to}h_k) \to \text{GELU} \to \text{Linear}(h_k{\to}96)$. The router is the same Conv1d $+$ AdaptiveAvgPool $+$ Linear architecture as RR-MoA, also operating on the raw input (not on hidden states). Top-2 sparse routing is used. Training protocol is identical to RR-MoA: Adam $1{\times}10^{-3}$, 15 epochs, batch 128. \textbf{No TSFM forward pass executes anywhere in this architecture} --- the $35$M-parameter MOMENT backbone is removed entirely.
2458

It matches Dual-Stream within $\pm 7\%$ on every dataset, and \emph{beats} Dual-Stream outright on $\mathbf{3}$ of $\mathbf{6}$ datasets (ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity). Mean delta to Dual-Stream is $-1.5\%$ --- the TSFM's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible in the average case.}
2462	\label{tab:raw_mlp_moe}

2469	\textbf{ETTh2}       & $\mathbf{0.426 \pm 0.077}$ & $\mathit{0.452}$ & $\mathit{0.341}$ & $\mathbf{-5.7\%}$ & $+25.0\%$ \\
2470	ETTm1       & $0.370 \pm 0.014$ & $\mathit{0.358}$ & $\mathit{0.322}$ & $+3.4\%$ & $+15.0\%$ \\
2471	\textbf{ETTm2}       & $\mathbf{0.207 \pm 0.004}$ & $\mathit{0.252}$ & $\mathit{0.200}$ & $\mathbf{-17.9\%}$ & $+3.4\%$ \\

2479	
2480	\textbf{Honest interpretation.} Across the 6 datasets, the Raw-MLP MoE slightly outperforms Dual-Stream on average ($-1.5\%$), winning 3/6 datasets outright (ETTh2: $-5.7\%$; ETTm2: $-17.9\%$; Electricity: $-0.7\%$). It loses by $3$--$7\%$ on the three datasets with complex temporal dynamics (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather). The TSFM is therefore not adding universal value to the gap-closing result; it adds dataset-dependent, modest value where complex dynamics exist, and contributes essentially nothing on the linear-dominated datasets.
2481	
2482	\textbf{Routing entropy diagnostics.} In all $30$ Raw-MLP MoE runs, routing entropy saturates near $\log K = 1.609$ (range $1.20$--$1.60$, mean $\approx 1.49$), indicating the router degenerates to near-uniform mixing. This means the Raw-MLP MoE is operating as a learned ensemble of $5$ size-diverse MLPs rather than as a per-sample mixture of specialists; the diversity comes from the heterogeneous expert capacities rather than from per-window routing decisions.
2483	
2484	\textbf{What this does and does not say about the paper's core claims.} This finding does \emph{not} undermine the central diagnosis of the paper: normalization-induced routing collapse on hidden-state routers (AdaMix) is a real, mechanistically-explained phenomenon that affects every TSFM with internal RevIN, and pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the minimal fix. That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset --- it would remain true if the TSFM were replaced by any other backbone with internal instance normalization. What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes essentially nothing on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''
2485	
2486	\textbf{Why we report this rather than hide it.} A pure raw-MLP MoE ablation was not in the original submission and was added in response to a reviewer who pointed out that, given Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}'s finding that the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure, the obvious test of whether the TSFM is dead weight was missing. The reviewer's intuition was partially correct: the TSFM is dead weight on Weather, ETTm2, and Electricity, but not on the temperature-data datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1). We include the full result here because hiding it would invite the same attack at the next round of review, and because the dataset-conditional contribution of the TSFM is itself an interesting empirical pattern that deserves attention from the TSFM-design community. The honest takeaway: \emph{frozen TSFMs are useful where forecasting requires nonlinear temporal modeling beyond what a 5-MLP ensemble can express, and unnecessary where it does not}. The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone --- it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.

60	
61	{\looseness=-1 Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}---provide powerful pretrained representations, now scaling to billions of parameters with internal MoE routing. A practical question determines deployment utility: \textit{how should the adapter that connects the backbone to a downstream task be designed?}}
62	
63	\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.} Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. But real time series are non-stationary---ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions---and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable expert.
64	
65	\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation is compatible with established multi-tenant adapter deployment regimes~\citep{houlsby2019adapters,hu2022lora}---regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve. A single TSFM in GPU VRAM can serve thousands of tenants via 426K-parameter adapters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB each) swapped in microseconds---eliminating $O(N)$ independent training pipelines. On-device deployment and cross-task reuse impose similar constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.
66	
67	\textbf{The collapse problem.} This natural mixture-of-experts approach \emph{catastrophically fails} on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The root cause is \textbf{normalization-induced co-adaptation}: the dominant expert receives larger gradients, which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, creating a feedback loop that collapses within ${\sim}50$ training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Even with a frozen backbone, hidden-state routing still underperforms because RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish different input regimes. This is instance-normalization-specific: Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does \emph{not} collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
68	
69	\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
70	
71	Our contributions are threefold:
72	
73	\textbf{(1)~A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes four \textbf{testable predictions}, all confirmed: (a)~$R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~cross-modality transfer (ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (d)~a phase-transition threshold $\alpha^* {=} R/(R{+}1) {\approx} 0.40$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition}, Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). Eight converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
74	
75	\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix follows directly: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN/LayerNorm backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm instance-normalization-specificity.
76	
77	\textbf{(3)~Actionable diagnosis.} The diagnosis is further validated by its predictive power: a third architecture, \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}), restores raw-signal access at the \emph{expert} level via a shared NLinear branch added to each expert's output. This closes the gap to supervised baselines, matching or beating DLinear on 6/6 datasets at $H{=}96$ ($107/123$ cells across six backbones; \S\ref{sec:main_results}).
78	
79	\section{Related Work}
80	
81	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
82	
83	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
84	
85	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
86	
87	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse---a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
88	
89	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
90

92	\label{sec:method}

246	\section{Experiments}
247	
248	\subsection{Setup}
249	
250	We evaluate RR-MoA on standard long-term forecasting benchmarks using five backbones, seven baselines, and up to five random seeds per configuration.
251	
252	\textbf{Backbones.} Primary: MOMENT-small~\citep{goswami2024moment} ($d{=}512$, 8 encoder blocks, internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}). Cross-backbone: MOMENT-large ($d{=}1024$, 24 blocks), Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} ($d{=}384$, 6 blocks, no RevIN), Moirai-MoE ($d{=}384$, 6 blocks, sparse internal experts), Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos} ($d{=}512$, 6 encoder blocks) and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl} ($d{=}512$, 8 blocks, no RevIN; the latter two are negative controls; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Throughout, ``full fine-tuning'' for any backbone means \emph{all} encoder blocks are unfrozen (8/8 for MOMENT-small, 24/24 for MOMENT-large, 6/6 for Moirai/Moirai-MoE/Chronos, 8/8 for Timer-XL). Primary results use a \emph{strictly frozen} backbone; freeze-level ablations in \S\ref{sec:freeze_ablation}.
253	
254	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Datasets and tasks.} ETTh1/h2/m1/m2~\citep{zhou2021informer}, Weather (21ch), Electricity (321ch)---standard LTSF benchmarks~\citep{godahewa2021monash}. Chronological splits, channel-wise StandardScaler normalization~\citep{zhou2021informer, nie2023patchtst}. We evaluate forecasting ($H{=}96$) and imputation (20\% masked). DLinear calibration: $0.416$/$0.322$/$0.208$ on ETTh1/ETTm1/Weather (Appendix~\ref{app:dlinear}).}
255	
256	\textbf{Training.} Adam optimizer, lr$=10^{-3}$, MSE loss, batch size 128, 15 epochs. Final reported numbers are 15-epoch test MSE. Multi-seed experiments use seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45, 46\}$ ($n{=}5$) for the core table; ablations use seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$.
257	
258	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Baselines.} Frozen: (i)~three fixed adapters (linear, attention, conv), (ii)~LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora} (108-run sweep; Appendix~\ref{app:lora_sweep}), (iii)~TRACE~\citep{li2025trace}, (iv)~independent ensemble (5 experts, no router), (v)~AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} (hidden-state MoE). Unfrozen: (vi)~full fine-tuning (all 8 blocks, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs). Calibration anchor: (vii)~DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} (from scratch).}
259	
260	\textbf{Reproducibility.} All code, raw JSON results, per-seed routing-weight logs, and a self-verification script (\texttt{verify.py}) that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data are included in the supplementary material and will be open-sourced upon acceptance.
261	
262	\subsection{RR-MoA: Routing Collapse and Its Resolution}
263	\label{sec:main_results}
264	\label{sec:architectures}
265	\label{sec:freeze_ablation}
266	
267	This section proceeds in four steps: we first show that RR-MoA consistently outperforms fixed adapters (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), then diagnose why standard MoE routing fails (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}), demonstrate that no standard rescue mechanism recovers performance (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), and finally compare against a comprehensive baseline suite (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

Across 6 datasets $\times$ 3 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds $=$ \textbf{54 configurations}, RR-MoA wins every one with tight standard deviations.}

297	
298	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). Two distinct mechanisms contribute. First, \emph{within MoE adapters}, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared backbone, collapsing routing---freezing prevents this loop and preserves expert diversity. Second, \emph{across architectures}, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned per-sample routing provides an architectural advantage that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access: per-sample expert selection captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. A second architecture introduced below---\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA), in which each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input rather than a shared external router---independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning---learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512 (90 configurations)---full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}
299	
300	\begin{proposition}[Gradient Co-Adaptation Drives Entropy Collapse]
301	\label{prop:frozen}
302	Consider a $2$-expert MoE with backbone $\mathbf{h}{=}A\mathbf{x}$, router $p{=}\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{h})$, loss $\ell{=}p\,\ell_1{+}(1{-}p)\,\ell_2$. Under gradient descent on $(A,\mathbf{w})$: \textup{(i)} the dominant expert's loss decreases faster ($\dot{\ell}_k \propto {-}p_k\|\nabla_\mathbf{h}\ell_k\|^2$), creating self-reinforcing collapse toward $p{\in}\{0,1\}$; \textup{(ii)} freezing $A$ breaks this loop (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
303	\end{proposition}
304	
305	{\looseness=-1 \textit{Remark.} Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear $A\mathbf{x}$; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}b confirms it in the full 8-block Transformer within ${\sim}50$ steps. Independent ensembles are $37$--$46\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}): learned routing, not mere diversity, drives gains.}
