337	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why does standard MoE routing fail?} To understand the source of RR-MoA's advantage, we examine AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}, which uses the standard recipe of routing on hidden states. Table~\ref{tab:adamix} shows that AdaMix collapses to a single expert whenever backbone layers are unfrozen: entropy reaches $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations; the remaining 5 stay below $0.55$ (vs.\ max ${\approx}1.61$) with high cross-seed variance ($\sigma$ up to $0.71$), indicating stochastic collapse rather than stable partial routing. The green rows reveal the cause: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy from $0.000$ to $0.66$--$1.32$, proving that normalization is the causal mechanism (BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm produce the same collapse; Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}). The causal contrast is sharpest when comparing backbones directly (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}): under identical last-4 unfreezing on identical data, MOMENT entropy crashes to $0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps while Timer-XL (which lacks RevIN) stays at $1.60$ for all $400$ steps---opposite trajectories from the same code.}

356	In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $27\%$ to $77\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
357	
358	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep five standard MoE rescue families---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across eleven configurations on 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate.
359	
360	\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants---all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router---each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual---this closes the DLinear gap.
361	
362	\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic (SR-MoA).} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, SR-MoA~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree} replaces the external Conv1d router with a per-expert sigmoid gate $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$---no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. A third architecture-level control, \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}), replaces AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. All three router instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) confirm the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight converging controls.

385	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why the simplicity of the fix is the point.} Identifying the correct cause is the hard part; that the fix follows trivially from the diagnosis is itself evidence the causal mechanism was correctly identified. The MoE community has long treated routing collapse as an \emph{optimization} problem---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss all attack the training dynamics---and these succeed when the router's input is informative but under-optimized. We show that normalization-induced collapse is a fundamentally different, \emph{information} problem: the routing signal is absent from the hidden states entirely, and none of the five rescue families (eleven configurations) we tested can compensate (720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}).}

416	
417	\textbf{Closing the DLinear gap.} DLinear (49K params, from scratch) outperforms frozen adapters in absolute MSE (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, grey rows). As the diagnosis predicts, restoring raw-signal access \emph{at the expert level} closes this gap: \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (a dual-stream architecture in which a shared NLinear raw-input branch is added to each expert's output; Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}) matches or beats DLinear on \textbf{6/6 datasets} at $H{=}96$ (up to $-7.5\%$), generalizing to $107/123$ cells across six backbones.\label{tab:gap_closing_headline}
418	
419	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass and dose-response.} Replacing the router's raw input with RevIN-normalized input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$ while entropy stays high (Table~\ref{tab:router_input}, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}), confirming the router relies on the \emph{content} of the stripped statistics, not merely the bypass path. A dose-response interpolation $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$ reveals a \emph{phase transition} (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs): MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), while entropy stays in $[1.43, 1.57]$---normalization renders routing uninformative without reducing diversity. The phase transition threshold is quantitatively predicted at $\alpha^* = R(\mathcal{D})/(R(\mathcal{D})+1) \approx 0.40$ for the median benchmark (Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}). A temporal-shuffle ablation confirms routing depends on $(M,\Sigma)$ statistics, not temporal ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}

479	
480	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experimental evidence above converges on a clear mechanism, but relies on empirical observations. We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into three components: mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$, discarding $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$. The following decomposition, while algebraically elementary (it follows from the MI chain rule), provides the formal basis for three testable quantitative predictions that we validate across nine datasets.
481	
482	\begin{observation}[Routing Information Loss Under Instance Normalization]
483	\label{thm:mi_decomp}
484	Let $X$ be a random input window, $E \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ the expert assignment produced by any deterministic router, and $S = (X - M)/\Sigma$ the RevIN-normalized shape.
485	\begin{enumerate}
486	    \item[\textup{(i)}] \textbf{Exact decomposition.} $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S) \geq 0$.
487	    \item[\textup{(ii)}] \textbf{Unconditional quantitative bound.} Without any independence assumption,
488	    \[
489	        I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;\geq\; I(M, \Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M, \Sigma;\, S),
490	    \]
491	    where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M, \Sigma;\, S) \geq 0$ measures the ``leakage'' of stripped statistics through the shape.  Equality (tightness) holds iff $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ given $E$.
492	    \item[\textup{(iii)}] \textbf{Full-information corner.} If the router depends \emph{entirely} on the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), then $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the \emph{entire} routing distribution in nats.
493	    \item[\textup{(iv)}] \textbf{Signal ratio as sufficient-statistic proxy.} Since Part~(iii) establishes that $(M,\Sigma)$ are sufficient statistics for $E$ when the router depends entirely on them, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ measures the variance contribution of these sufficient statistics relative to the residual shape---a monotone proxy for the \emph{potential} routing information in the stripped statistics. The leakage $\varepsilon$ varies by dataset ($0.09$--$1.26$ nats via CCA; cross-validated within ${\pm}0.2$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}); $R(\mathcal{D})$ is validated at $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ across nine datasets. \textbf{Tightness:} direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via held-out classifier confirms normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy; the bound~(ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}).\footnote{$H(E \mid S)$ does not correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$); $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts improvement because it measures routing \emph{potential}, not the MI loss itself.}
494	\end{enumerate}
495	\end{observation}
496	
497	Full proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}; rate-distortion interpretation and phase-transition formalization in Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}. \textit{Remark.} KSG cross-check (${\pm}0.26$ nats) confirms leakage estimates hold beyond Gaussianity. \textbf{Independent validation:} training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as an \texttt{nn.Parameter}, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}).
498	
499	\textbf{Quantitative prediction.} The \emph{routing signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\text{Var}(S)}$ measures whether input windows in a dataset differ primarily in their location and scale (high $R$, normalization destroys the dominant routing signal) or primarily in their shape (low $R$, routing signal survives normalization). It serves as a monotone proxy for the MI bound. Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} validates this: the Spearman rank correlation between $R(\mathcal{D})$ and the MSE improvement $\Delta\%$ from raw routing is $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI: $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$), i.e., datasets where normalization strips more routing signal benefit more from bypassing it. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier: the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.

574	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone} RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). On Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins \textbf{18/18} by $3$--$31\%$---demonstrating that raw-signal routing provides value \emph{beyond} the RevIN diagnosis: even when hidden states retain enough information to avoid collapse (Moirai entropy: $1.48$--$1.60$), the raw input carries richer per-window statistics that improve routing quality. On Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, which already contains sparse internal experts, RR-MoA still improves \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $37$--$90\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}), showing that adapter-level and backbone-internal routing operate on complementary axes. Two \textbf{negative controls} validate the diagnosis: Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, which lack instance normalization, show no routing collapse (entropy $1.48$--$1.61$) and RR-MoA provides no advantage (\textbf{4/18} wins, within chance)---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}).}
575	
576	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Sparse routing and task generalization.}\label{sec:topk}
577	Top-2 sparse routing adds $4.3$\,ms ($+10\%$) while retaining $63\%$ of the dense gain; scaling $K{=}3{\to}20$ changes MSE by ${<}5\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:topk}). RR-MoA generalizes to imputation ($7/8$ datasets; Appendix~\ref{app:imputation}).}
578	
579	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Multi-horizon generalization.} RR-MoA wins \textbf{24/24} configurations across $H{\in}\{96, 192, 336, 720\}$ on ETTh1, ETTm1, and Weather (5 seeds each; Table~\ref{tab:horizon}), with improvements of $27$--$49\%$ over the best fixed adapter at every horizon. The advantage is stable across horizon length: at $H{=}720$, RR-MoA still improves by $27$--$41\%$. \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}) further extends this to all 6 datasets across 5 backbones and 4 horizons (Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}

581	\vspace{-0.5em}
582	\section{Conclusion}
583	\vspace{-0.3em}
584	
585	We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} as the root cause of MoE adapter failure on time series foundation models. Eight causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: \textbf{RR-MoA} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. The diagnosis is further validated by its actionability: restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones.
586	
587	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: in our 9 LTSF benchmarks, values above $0.5$ reliably predict raw routing helps (6/6 datasets, $27$--$77\%$ improvement). Below $0.2$ the prediction is one-sided: Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted to not benefit, but Solar ($R{=}0.06$, $\Delta{=}{-}32.9\%$) does benefit because the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale (SSR ablation, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}). $R(\mathcal{D})$ thus captures a sufficient (not necessary) condition for raw routing to help; high $R$ is a strong positive predictor, while low $R$ does not rule out gains from richer temporal structure. \textbf{Limitations:} Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested; Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear backbones only (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers); $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first moments and may miss higher-order routing signals (Solar outlier).

211	\subsection{Problem Formulation and Expert Pool}
212	
213	For a mixture of adapters to be effective, the expert pool must contain structurally diverse heads so that the router has meaningful choices. An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
214	
215	\textbf{Standard protocol.} Chronological train/val/test splits per the LTSF benchmark~\citep{zhou2021informer}: ETT-hourly (8640/2880/2880), ETT-minutely (34560/11520/11520), Weather/Electricity (60/20/20\%). Final evaluation uses the held-out test set.
216	
217	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
218	\label{sec:rrmoa}

337	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why does standard MoE routing fail?} To understand the source of RR-MoA's advantage, we examine AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}, which uses the standard recipe of routing on hidden states. Table~\ref{tab:adamix} shows that AdaMix collapses to a single expert whenever backbone layers are unfrozen: entropy reaches $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations; the remaining 5 stay below $0.55$ (vs.\ max ${\approx}1.61$) with high cross-seed variance ($\sigma$ up to $0.71$), indicating stochastic collapse rather than stable partial routing. The green rows reveal the cause: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy from $0.000$ to $0.66$--$1.32$, proving that normalization is the causal mechanism (BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm produce the same collapse; Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}). The causal contrast is sharpest when comparing backbones directly (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}): under identical last-4 unfreezing on identical data, MOMENT entropy crashes to $0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps while Timer-XL (which lacks RevIN) stays at $1.60$ for all $400$ steps---opposite trajectories from the same code.}

385	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why the simplicity of the fix is the point.} Identifying the correct cause is the hard part; that the fix follows trivially from the diagnosis is itself evidence the causal mechanism was correctly identified. The MoE community has long treated routing collapse as an \emph{optimization} problem---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss all attack the training dynamics---and these succeed when the router's input is informative but under-optimized. We show that normalization-induced collapse is a fundamentally different, \emph{information} problem: the routing signal is absent from the hidden states entirely, and none of the five rescue families (eleven configurations) we tested can compensate (720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}).}

It also explicitly motivates `app:raw_mlp_moe` (Claim D). The Ridge/RF prose is redundant once you have the headline k-NN comparison; the few-shot table is still load-bearing. **Trim, don't cut.**

- **`app:routing_weights` (§F)** — Marginally relevant. Shows routing is dataset-diverse rather than collapsed/random. `tab:self_routed` and `fig:routing_viz` already convey this. **Defensible to drop entirely.**

- **`app:expert_count` (§K.2)** — Yes. The K-scaling robustness claim ("K=3→20 changes MSE by <5%") is made in §4 main text; this section provides the data for it. **Merge into `app:topk`, do not cut.**

**Vestigial within an otherwise-relevant section**:

- **FFT-Router / SAIB / IA-Gating sub-paragraphs in `app:routing_ablations`** — These are negative-result probes from earlier exploration. None test alternatives that a reasonable reviewer would propose ("did you try…?"). They neither support nor falsify the diagnosis. **Genuinely off-narrative; drop them.**

**Promote-or-cut, both relevant**:

- **`app:sr_ria` (§T.2)** — The SR-MoA × Residual-IA⁺ stack reaching 6/6 is a real result that strengthens the paper. The architecture-agnostic story argues this *is* relevant. Currently invisible because no main-text pointer. **Promote with a sentence, don't cut.**

- **`app:raw_mlp_moe` (§T.3)** — Directly defends Claim D against the "TSFM is dead weight" attack. **Highly relevant; promote with a main-text pointer.**

So: nothing in the trim list is *off-narrative* in the strong sense those three deleted sections were. The trim recommendations are about *length-vs-value*, not relevance. If you'd rather keep all of them at full length and only act on the three already-deleted, that's a defensible call too — the appendix is at 2445 lines, not blowing past any hard limit.

# RACE VM SSH Access

## Connection command
```bash
ssh -i hungphanphd.pem ec2-user@ec2-13-238-161-176.ap-southeast-2.compute.amazonaws.com
```

- **Key**: `hungphanphd.pem` (in repo root)
- **User**: `ec2-user`
- **Host**: `ec2-13-238-161-176.ap-southeast-2.compute.amazonaws.com`
- **GPU**: NVIDIA A10G (23GB VRAM), CUDA 12.4
- **OS**: Ubuntu 22.04 on AWS (kernel 6.8.0)

## IP whitelisting

SSH access requires your public IP in the RACE security group (port 22).

To update:
1. Get your current IP: `curl ifconfig.me`
2. Professor logs into https://race.rmit.edu.au
3. Workspaces → select workspace → **Edit Security Group**
4. Add `<your-ip>/32` on **port 22**

## Permanent SSH Access (bypasses 60-second window)

The public key has been added to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the VM, so SSH works anytime without needing to click "Use this SSH Key" in RACE. This was done by:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
echo '<public-key>' > ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

To re-extract the public key from the `.pem` if needed:
```bash
ssh-keygen -y -f hungphanphd.pem
```

## Notes
- Key permissions must be `chmod 400` (`chmod 400 hungphanphd.pem`)

### Safety nets still in place
- **Backup branch `backup-pre-scrub-20260428`** exists locally and on `origin` and `henry`. Holds the pre-rewrite tip (`c93c819`). Delete when you're confident the new history is good (`git push origin --delete backup-pre-scrub-20260428`).
- All scrubbed files still exist **on your local disk** — only their git history was removed.

### Overleaf — what you need to do

Overleaf's GitHub-sync tracks history. After a force-push it will see divergent history and refuse a normal pull. Pick one:

**Option 1 — Cleanest (recommended).** In Overleaf:
1. Open the project → Menu → **Sync → GitHub**
2. Click **Disconnect / Unlink GitHub**
3. Wait a few seconds, then **Re-link** the project to the same GitHub repo. Overleaf will treat it as a fresh import and pick up the new clean history. Any uncommitted Overleaf-side edits will be lost — make sure you've synced them out first.

**Option 2 — Force pull (if your Overleaf plan supports it).** Some Overleaf paid plans expose a "Force pull from GitHub" option in the same Sync menu. That fast-forwards Overleaf to the new history without re-importing.

**Option 3 — Manual reset (most control).** If you have shell access to the Overleaf project's git checkout: `git fetch origin && git reset --hard origin/main`. Most cloud Overleaf users don't have this; only relevant if you self-host or use the CLI bridge.

- The VM's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` (per the old `RACE_SSH.md` notes, the public key was added there for permanent access) is unchanged. The VM doesn't know or care what happens to GitHub's history.

If you consider that sensitive, you'd need to rotate the SSH key on the VM (regenerate, replace `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, get a new `.pem`). But normal connectivity from your machine using the existing key works exactly as before.

\newlabel{fig:framework}{{1}{4}{\textbf {RR-MoA architecture.} \textit {Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$ (no gradients through $\theta $); all experts receive $\mathbf {H}$. \textit {Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf {H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm }0.000$; Table~\ref {tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf {54/54 wins} (Table~\ref {tab:rrmoa})}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:trajectory}{{2}{7}{\textbf {Per-step routing / gradient trajectory} (AdaMix, ETTh1). (a)~Unfrozen+RevIN (red) collapses within ${\sim }50$ steps; frozen (blue) stays stable. Unfrozen \emph {without} RevIN (green dashed) also stays stable. (b)~Dominant expert's gradient grows while others starve (co-adaptation loop, \S \ref {sec:rrmoa})}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:causal_contrast}{{3}{7}{\textbf {Causal contrast: MOMENT vs Timer-XL} (ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing). MOMENT entropy collapses $0.51{\to }0.000$ in ${\sim }40$ steps (red); Timer-XL stays at ${\approx }1.60$ for all $400$ steps (orange). Same code, same data, only normalization differs. Pattern generalizes across all 3 tested datasets}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:dose_response}{{4}{9}{\textbf {Normalization dose-response} (frozen, 5 seeds $\times $ 6 datasets). \textbf {Left:} MSE vs $\alpha $ ($0{=}$raw, $1{=}$RevIN). Phase transition at $\alpha {=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), mild for $\alpha {\leq }0.75$ ($+5.4\%$). \textbf {Right:} entropy stays high at all $\alpha $---normalization renders routing uninformative, not collapsed}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:frozen_paradox}{{5}{10}{\textbf {Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf {Right: Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:signal_ratio}{{5}{10}{\textbf {Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf {Right: Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_appendix}{{E1}{20}{\textbf {Multi-seed RR-MoA routing weights per dataset} (Top-2 sparse, strictly frozen, mean$\pm $std over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$). Routing is diverse and dataset-dependent: ETTh1 spreads weight roughly uniformly (entropy $1.495\pm 0.034$); ETTm1 concentrates on Last+Max; Weather on Mean+Conv1d}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:collapse_mechanism}{{F2}{20}{\textbf {Normalization-induced routing collapse mechanism.} \textit {Left:} Raw input windows with distinct characteristics (amplitude, trend, volatility) are routed to different experts. \textit {Right:} After instance normalization strips $\mu $ and $\sigma $, all windows become indistinguishable, and the router collapses to a single expert (entropy $\to 0.000$)}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:srmoa_arch}{{F3}{21}{\textbf {SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma _k$ reading $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf {H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph {raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref {fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_viz}{{F4}{21}{\textbf {Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma ) \perp \!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp}(iii)}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:residual_ia_arch}{{R5}{28}{\textbf {Residual-IA\textsuperscript {+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit {Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit {Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf {y}_k = \mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw} + \sigma (\mathrm {blend}_k(\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw})) \cdot \mathrm {Adapter}_k(\mathbf {H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma $ gates (orange) on $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf {6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf {107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times $ 6 datasets $\times $ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref {tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref {tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb})}{figure.5}{}}

"""T2.A visualization: plot per-step routing / gradient trajectories
produced by ``run_adamix.py --trajectory ...``.

Reads two JSONL files (an "unfrozen" collapse case and a "frozen" control)
and produces a single two-panel figure:

    Panel (a): routing entropy over optimizer steps, one line per setting.
    Panel (b): per-expert gradient L2 norm over steps, collapse case only
               (to show that one expert's gradient dominates and the others
               rapidly starve). A dashed line gives the sum of the other 4
               experts for reference.

Usage::

    python scripts/plot_adamix_trajectory.py \
        --collapse results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_last4_42.jsonl \
        --control  results/adamix/trajectory_ETTh1_frozen_42.jsonl \
        --out figures/adamix_trajectory.pdf

The output PDF is intended to be dropped into ``main.tex`` as a standalone
figure between Tables 4 and 5, upgrading the gradient co-adaptation claim
from correlational (Table 4 entropies at epoch end) to mechanistic.
"""

import argparse
import json
import math
import os
import sys

import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def load_jsonl(path):
    records = []
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            records.append(json.loads(line))
    return records


def plot_trajectory(collapse_path, control_path, out_path, K=5):
    collapse = load_jsonl(collapse_path)
    control = load_jsonl(control_path) if control_path else None

    max_steps = max(len(collapse), len(control) if control else 0)
    log_max = math.log(K)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.3), dpi=150)

    # --- Panel (a): routing entropy over steps ---
    ax = axes[0]
    steps_c = [r["step"] for r in collapse]
    ent_c = [r["routing_entropy"] for r in collapse]
```

480	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experimental evidence above converges on a clear mechanism, but relies on empirical observations. We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into three components: mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$, discarding $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$. The following decomposition, while algebraically elementary (it follows from the MI chain rule), provides the formal basis for three testable quantitative predictions that we validate across nine datasets.

573	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone} RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). On Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins \textbf{18/18} by $3$--$31\%$---demonstrating that raw-signal routing provides value \emph{beyond} the RevIN diagnosis: even when hidden states retain enough information to avoid collapse (Moirai entropy: $1.48$--$1.60$), the raw input carries richer per-window statistics that improve routing quality. On Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, which already contains sparse internal experts, RR-MoA still improves \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $37$--$90\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}), showing that adapter-level and backbone-internal routing operate on complementary axes. Two \textbf{negative controls} validate the diagnosis: Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, which lack instance normalization, show no routing collapse (entropy $1.48$--$1.61$) and RR-MoA provides no advantage (\textbf{4/18} wins, within chance)---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}).}

\newlabel{fig:framework}{{1}{4}{\textbf {RR-MoA architecture.} \textit {Path~A} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$ (no gradients through $\theta $); all experts receive $\mathbf {H}$. \textit {Path~B} (orange): a lightweight Conv1d gate (1{,}100 params) reads the raw pre-normalization signal $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ and selects the Top-2 experts via sparse routing. Only the selected experts (bold) contribute to the output; inactive experts (gray) receive no gradient. Standard MoE routing on $\mathbf {H}$ collapses (entropy $0.000{\pm }0.000$; Table~\ref {tab:adamix}); RR-MoA achieves \textbf {54/54 wins} (Table~\ref {tab:rrmoa})}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:trajectory}{{2}{7}{\textbf {Per-step routing / gradient trajectory} (AdaMix, ETTh1). (a)~Unfrozen+RevIN (red) collapses within ${\sim }50$ steps; strictly frozen control (blue) stays stable, isolating gradient co-adaptation from optimizer or data effects. (b)~Dominant expert's gradient grows while others starve (co-adaptation loop, \S \ref {sec:rrmoa}). Removing RevIN (separate experiment, Figure~\ref {fig:causal_contrast}) shows the trajectory inverts}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:causal_contrast}{{3}{7}{\textbf {Causal contrast: MOMENT vs Timer-XL} (ETTh1, last-4 unfreezing). MOMENT entropy collapses $0.51{\to }0.000$ in ${\sim }40$ steps (red); Timer-XL stays at ${\approx }1.60$ for all $400$ steps (orange). Same code, same data, only normalization differs. Pattern generalizes across all 3 tested datasets}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:dose_response}{{4}{9}{\textbf {Normalization dose-response} (frozen, 5 seeds $\times $ 6 datasets). \textbf {Left:} MSE vs $\alpha $ ($0{=}$raw, $1{=}$RevIN). Phase transition at $\alpha {=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), mild for $\alpha {\leq }0.75$ ($+5.4\%$). \textbf {Right:} entropy stays high at all $\alpha $---normalization renders routing uninformative, not collapsed}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:frozen_paradox}{{5}{10}{\textbf {Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf {Right: Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:signal_ratio}{{5}{10}{\textbf {Left: Frozen Paradox}---frozen RR-MoA beats full FT by $12$--$79\%$. \textbf {Right: Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp} validated} ($\rho {=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$). Traffic and Solar are boundary cases}{figure.5}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_appendix}{{E1}{20}{\textbf {Multi-seed RR-MoA routing weights per dataset} (Top-2 sparse, strictly frozen, mean$\pm $std over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$). Routing is diverse and dataset-dependent: ETTh1 spreads weight roughly uniformly (entropy $1.495\pm 0.034$); ETTm1 concentrates on Last+Max; Weather on Mean+Conv1d}{figure.1}{}}
\newlabel{fig:collapse_mechanism}{{F2}{20}{\textbf {Normalization-induced routing collapse mechanism.} \textit {Left:} Raw input windows with distinct characteristics (amplitude, trend, volatility) are routed to different experts. \textit {Right:} After instance normalization strips $\mu $ and $\sigma $, all windows become indistinguishable, and the router collapses to a single expert (entropy $\to 0.000$)}{figure.2}{}}
\newlabel{fig:srmoa_arch}{{F3}{21}{\textbf {SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma _k$ reading $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly---no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf {H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph {raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref {fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains}{figure.3}{}}
\newlabel{fig:routing_viz}{{F4}{21}{\textbf {Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma ) \perp \!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref {thm:mi_decomp}(iii)}{figure.4}{}}
\newlabel{fig:residual_ia_arch}{{R5}{28}{\textbf {Residual-IA\textsuperscript {+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit {Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf {H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit {Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf {y}_k = \mathbf {y}_\mathrm {raw} + \sigma (\mathrm {blend}_k(\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw})) \cdot \mathrm {Adapter}_k(\mathbf {H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma $ gates (orange) on $\mathbf {X}_\mathrm {raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf {6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf {107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times $ 6 datasets $\times $ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref {tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref {tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb})}{figure.5}{}}

SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle---not the specific router---drives the gains.}

2127	\caption{\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} architecture (dual-stream extension).} \textit{Stream 1} (blue): the frozen TSFM produces hidden states $\mathbf{H}$, fed into each expert's Adapter head. \textit{Stream 2} (green): a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$ so the model starts as effectively-DLinear and learns to add backbone signal where useful. Self-routing $\sigma$ gates (orange) on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ select which experts contribute. Result: \textbf{6/6 vs DLinear at $H{=}96$} on MOMENT-small; \textbf{107/123 cells} ($88\%$) match-or-beat across 6 backbones $\times$ 6 datasets $\times$ 4 horizons (Tables~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus}, \ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}
2128	\label{fig:residual_ia_arch}
2129	\end{figure}
2130	
2131	The dual-stream and multi-resolution variants narrow the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5$--$8\%$ (Tables~\ref{tab:gap_closing}, \ref{tab:gap_closing_ext}) but win on only 1/6 datasets (Weather). A systematic $546$-run hyperparameter sweep uncovered a \emph{second} hidden pathology and the architectural fix that closes the remaining gap to \textbf{4/6 match-or-beat}.
2132	
2133	\textbf{Diagnostic: gates fail to learn.} We instrumented the per-sample gate mechanism to log its mean activation per expert per dataset. Across every configuration tested---\{rh128, rh192, rh256, rh320, rh384, rh512\} $\times$ \{d1, d2, d3 raw-branch depth\} $\times$ \{lr, wd, cosine, warmup\} hyperparameter combinations---the learned gates consistently plateau at $\sigma(0.0){\approx}0.5$:
